title: Silas and the Postcards
premise: Felix Voss, a translator who has spent twelve years translating away from her mother tongue rather than toward it, learns that the house where she grew up with her grandmother — a woman who never left, and whom Felix never returned to — is being auctioned and demolished. Returning to settle the estate, she discovers a shoebox of unsent postcards her grandmother wrote to her every month for twelve years, each one ending mid-sentence. As developers circle and old neighbors press her to sign quickly, Felix must decide whether loyalty to her grandmother's silence or the truth of her own grief will shape how she says goodbye. In the end, she reads the final unfinished postcard aloud at the auction itself, buys back only the front door as salvage, and speaks her goodbye in the fading language — finishing her grandmother's last sentence with words of her own.
about_author: August Quintana is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade between languages and now writes about the people who live in the gaps between them. Silas and the Postcards is their second novel, inspired by a box of letters found in a condemned farmhouse.

chapters.title: The Word That Wouldn't Come
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. In her city apartment, Felix fumbles a translation job, reaching for a childhood word that no longer surfaces, and receives the certified letter: the house on Alder Lane goes to auction in six weeks. She almost throws it away. Emotional beat: denial dressed up as professional composure.

chapters.title: Alder Lane, Number Nine
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. She returns to the town she fled twelve years ago and finds the house boarded, the orchard half-felled, and the neighbor Marta waiting on the porch with questions Felix can't answer in either language. Emotional beat: the shock of a place that kept existing without her.

chapters.title: What the Auctioneer Knows
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, with a shift into auctioneer Dev Rennick's perspective midway. Dev, charming and ruthless, offers to expedite the sale — and mentions the demolition clause. Felix signs nothing but leaves shaken, realizing the town wants her gone more than it wants her back. Emotional beat: pressure disguised as kindness.

chapters.title: The Shoebox Under the Stairs
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Clearing the attic, she finds 144 unsent postcards addressed to her, one per month since she left, each breaking off mid-sentence. The last is dated three days before her grandmother Sila died. Emotional beat: vertigo — twelve years of love she never opened.

chapters.title: Marta Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Felix and Marta. Marta reveals that Sila refused to send the cards, believing a goodbye mailed was a goodbye finished, and that she'd been saving something for Felix's return. Felix resents the implication that leaving was abandonment. Emotional beat: loyalty and blame braided together.

chapters.title: Dev Makes It Easy
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev offers Felix above-market cash to sign fast, hinting the town council will fast-track demolition either way. Tempted by the clean exit, Felix nearly signs — then notices Dev's own hesitation about the orchard tree, a crack in his certainty. Emotional beat: power flexing, and its first hairline fracture.

chapters.title: Reading Backward
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Over sleepless nights she translates the postcards from her mother tongue into English and watches the language of them decay — Sila losing words too, substituting, circling, until the sentences fray. Felix realizes they were both going silent in parallel. Emotional beat: grief reframed as kinship.

chapters.title: The Tree They Can't Cut Yet
chapters.summary: Marta and Felix POV. The townspeople, led by Marta, petition to save the orchard's oldest tree; Dev, pressured by investors, refuses — until an inspection delays demolition by two weeks. Felix sees that delay is not victory, only room. Emotional beat: fragile hope, collective defiance.

chapters.title: The Last Unfinished Sentence
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, climax. On auction day, before the crowd and Dev's gavel, Felix stands on the porch and reads the final postcard aloud in her mother tongue, then finishes Sila's broken sentence in her own words — a real goodbye, out loud, public and irreversible. The room goes still; Dev lowers the gavel without striking it. Emotional beat: truth breaking through duty.

chapters.title: The Front Door
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, resolution. The house sells; demolition proceeds. Felix salvages only the front door, loads it into Marta's truck, and drives away speaking aloud in the fading language — not to preserve it, but to use it while it's hers. Final image: the door strapped in the truck bed like a passenger. Emotional beat: sorrow carried forward, not resolved away.
